nodes.name: Drastic Nonequilibrium Precipitation
nodes.procedure: Drastic nonequilibrium precipitation was proposed in this work to prepare OER catalysts with highly disordered crystal structures, which was simply performed by mixing high-concentration metal ions with a concentrated alkaline solution (1 M KOH). When high-concentration metal ions in an aqueous solution were added drop by drop into a concentrated alkaline solution (1 M KOH), drastic nonequilibrium precipitation occurs. The synthesis process is ultrafast and scalable.

unit_operations.name: Rapid Octahedron Formation
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: metal ions and OH⁻ ions formed [M^{II}(OH)₆]⁴⁻ or [M^{III}(OH)₆]³⁻ octahedrons quickly, surrounded by alkaline metal ions such as K⁺ for charge balance

unit_operations.name: Nonequilibrium Nucleation
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: nonequilibrium nucleation of octahedrons produced small LDH nanosheets with a large number of defect sites of octahedron units

unit_operations.name: Dropwise Addition Precipitation
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: high-concentration metal ions in an aqueous solution were added drop by drop into a concentrated alkaline solution (1 M KOH)

unit_operations.name: Nanosheet Assembly
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: small nanosheets would further assemble to form large-size nanosheets with a highly disordered crystal structure containing cationic defects

nodes.characterization_summary: Ultrathin two-dimensional (2D) nanosheets observed for d-NiFe-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As evidenced by TEM images in Figure 1g–k, all the as-prepared LDH materials are observed to be ultrathin two-dimensional (2D) nanosheets, and the SEM images further confirm their 2D structure (Figure S3).

nodes.characterization_summary: Highly disordered lattice fringes observed for d-NiFe-LDH, attributed to high density of cationic defects from missing metal-oxygen octahedron units; defects of different sizes correspond to mono-cationic, di-cationic, and multi-cationic defects.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The lattice fringes could be observed clearly in the typical HRTEM images (Figure 1l–p) for all the as-synthesized LDH materials. The lattice is highly disordered with barely observed straight fringes...

nodes.characterization_summary: d-NiFe-LDH shows broader characteristic diffraction peaks indicating reduced crystallinity compared to conventional NiFe-LDH; both assigned to single phase LDHs (JCPDS No. 38-0715).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the d -NiFe-LDH and the conventional NiFe-LDH sample were compared in Figure 3a. The positions of diffraction peaks for the two samples are almost the same...

nodes.characterization_summary: d-NiFe-LDH nanosheets thickness measured as ≈0.8 nm, indicating monolayer structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The thickness of the d -NiFe-LDH nanosheets measured by atomic force microscopy (AFM) is ≈0.8 nm (Figure 3b and c).

nodes.characterization_summary: d-NiFe-LDH shows K 2p signal confirming K presence (K/Ni atomic ratio ~1:10); Ni 2p3/2 peak upshifted by 0.8 eV compared to conventional NiFe-LDH, attributed to disordered crystal structure.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were conducted to investigate the composition of d -NiFe-LDH by comparing it with the conventional NiFe-LDH. Interestingly, the d -NiFe-LDH presents the signal of K element (Figure 3d)... quantitative analysis of the XPS results reveal that the atomic ratio of K/Ni is about 1:10 for the d -NiFe-LDH. In addition... an obvious upshift of 0.8 eV in the Ni 2p3/2 spectrum...

nodes.characterization_summary: d-NiFe-LDH shows lower weight loss temperatures for water removal (RT-≈180°C) and dehydroxylation (≈180-≈300°C); additional weight loss >700°C attributed to K2O volatilization.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Thermogravimetric analysis was deployed... the d -NiFe-LDH presents much lower temperatures for the two stages of weight loss... additional weight loss when the temperature increases over 700°C, which could be ascribed to the volatilization of K2O.

nodes.characterization_summary: d-NiFe-LDH shows water oxidation onset at 1.37 V without obvious Ni²⁺ oxidation peak (vs 1.45-1.50 V for conventional NiFe-LDH); cathodic peak at 1.24 V assigned to γ-NiOOH reduction (vs 1.34 V for β-NiOOH in conventional NiFe-LDH).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Cyclic voltammetry curves of the d -NiFe-LDH and the conventional NiFe-LDH are compared in Figure 3g. An oxidation peak at 1.45 - 1.50 V was observed... for the conventional NiFe-LDH sample... In contrast, the d -NiFe-LDH sample presents an onset potential at 1.37 V for water oxidation... a cathodic peak located at 1.34 V for the conventional NiFe-LDH can be assigned to the reduction of β -NiOOH, while the cathodic peak located at 1.24 V for the d -NiFe-LDH can be ascribed to the reduction of γ -NiOOH.

nodes.characterization_summary: d-NiFe-LDH possesses 1.45 mmol/g base sites; conventional NiFe-LDH has no base sites.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Acid-base titration indicates that the d -NiFe-LDH possesses a large number of base sites up to 1.45 mmol g-1, while the conventional NiFe-LDH has no base sites (Figure 3h).

nodes.characterization_summary: Spherical aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM confirms cationic defects with different sizes in d-NiFe-LDH.
nodes.evidence_snippet: And these cationic defects with different sizes could be further confirmed by spherical aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM image (Figure S4).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS analysis of d-NiFe-LDH indicates evenly distributed K⁺ ions, confirming K⁺ doping.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The EDS analysis of d -NiFe-LDH indicates the existence of evenly distributed K⁺ ions, which indicates the K⁺ doping in the samples induced by ultrafast formation of LDHs (Figure S5).
